title: Biggest Block of Ones After Shuffling Columns
statement:
You get a grid matrix of 0s and 1s. You may reorder its columns in any way you like (a column moves as a whole; rows keep their order).

After reordering, return the area of the largest rectangle that contains only 1s.

examples.why: Put columns 0 and 2 side by side: rows 1 and 2 are all 1s there, a 2 × 2 block. Column 0 alone gives a 3 × 1 block, area 3, so tallest is not best.
Move the three 1-columns together to get a 1 × 3 block.
No column has two 1s and no row has two 1s, so the best block is a single cell.

hints: Fix the bottom row of the rectangle. For each column, how many 1s are stacked directly above that row, including it?
With those column heights, column order is free. If you want a rectangle of height h, which columns can join, and where should you put them?
Sort the heights in a row from tallest to shortest. Taking the first k columns gives height heights[k − 1] and width k. Try every k on every row.

explain.intuition:
Pick the bottom row of the rectangle. For each column, count how many 1s stand in an unbroken stack ending at that row: that is the column's height. Swapping columns does not change these heights, because a column moves as a whole.

Now the order is yours to choose, so line the columns up from tallest to shortest. A rectangle that uses the k tallest columns can be as tall as the shortest of them, which is the k-th height in sorted order. Any other choice of k columns would be no taller. So for each row, the best area is the maximum of k · sorted[k − 1], and the answer is the best over all rows. It is the "largest rectangle in a histogram" problem, made easy because you are allowed to sort the bars.
steps: Keep an array h of column heights, starting at 0.
For each row: set h[j] = h[j] + 1 where the cell is 1, else h[j] = 0.
Copy h and sort it in decreasing order.
For every k, update the answer with k · sorted[k − 1].
pitfalls: Only taking the tallest column or only the widest row. In the first example neither gives 4.
Sorting h itself instead of a copy. The next row needs the heights in their original column positions.
Not resetting a height to 0 on a 0 cell: a column's stack has to be unbroken.

solutions.title: Try every band of rows
solutions.idea: For every top and bottom row, count the columns that are all 1s in between; those columns can be moved together.

solutions.title: Column heights, sorted per row
solutions.idea: Heights of the 1-stacks ending at each row; sorted from tallest, the k tallest give area k times the k-th height.

followups: Avoid the sort: keep the columns in height order from the previous row and update that order in O(cols) per row.
Now rows may be reordered instead of columns. Is it the same problem?
